title: M14, NGC 6402
caption: The globular cluster M14, imaged by the KPNO 0.9-meter telescope

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: This picture shows M14, also cataloged as NGC 6402, a globular cluster in the constellation Ophiuchus. Compared with many globular clusters it is somewhat loose, and it is very nearly circular on the sky, with only a very small ellipticity.
Ellipticity is a measure of how far an object's outline departs from a perfect circle. M14 lies about 29000 light-years away and is about 72 light-years across.

A globular cluster is a dense, roughly spherical collection of old stars held together by gravity. Clusters differ in how tightly their stars are packed, and looser ones like M14 let a telescope pick out individual stars farther toward the center. These clusters orbit our Galaxy and contain some of its oldest stars, so they are valuable for studying how the Milky Way formed and how stars grow old.
scale: M14 is about 29000 light-years away and about 72 light-years across, according to NOIRLab.

understand.summary: A CCD camera on the 0.9-meter telescope at Kitt Peak recorded M14 in visible light. The filters and color mapping are not published.
understand.eye: The camera's exposures gather far more light than the eye and resolve many of the cluster's individual stars.
